clinicalPearls: A pure motor palsy of the anterior interosseous nerve, the deep motor branch of the median nerve, causing weakness of flexor pollicis longus, flexor digitorum profundus to the index (and often middle) finger, and pronator quadratus, with NO sensory loss
The classic sign is inability to make a rounded 'OK' sign: the terminal thumb and index joints cannot flex, so pinch collapses into a flat, wide 'pinch attitude' (Kiloh-Nevin sign)
Pronator quadratus weakness is tested by resisted forearm pronation with the elbow fully flexed to neutralise the humeral head of pronator teres
Many cases are not true entrapment but a restricted form of neuralgic amyotrophy (Parsonage-Turner syndrome), typically heralded by acute severe forearm or shoulder-girdle pain preceding the weakness
True compressive causes include fibrous bands, an accessory head of flexor pollicis longus (Gantzer muscle), enlarged bursae or vessels, and mass lesions in the proximal forearm

It is distinguished from rupture of flexor pollicis longus or flexor digitorum profundus tendons, which is excluded by an intact tenodesis effect, and from carpal tunnel syndrome by the absence of sensory symptoms

Management is usually conservative with observation and physiotherapy given the high rate of spontaneous recovery, especially in inflammatory cases; surgical decompression is reserved for a demonstrable compressive lesion or lack of recovery over an extended period
reference.pathophysiology: The anterior interosseous nerve branches from the median nerve in the proximal forearm, usually just distal to the two heads of pronator teres, and runs on the interosseous membrane to supply flexor pollicis longus, the radial half of flexor digitorum profundus and pronator quadratus. Because it is purely motor, lesions produce a distinctive weakness of distal thumb and index-finger flexion and forearm pronation without any sensory deficit. Injury may result from external or internal compression by fibrous arcades, anomalous muscles or vessels and mass lesions, or, frequently, from an immune-mediated inflammatory process (neuralgic amyotrophy) that selectively involves the fascicles destined for the anterior interosseous nerve, producing hourglass-like nerve constrictions demonstrable on imaging.
additionalDifferentials: Neuralgic amyotrophy (Parsonage-Turner syndrome) with selective anterior interosseous involvement
Rupture of flexor pollicis longus or flexor digitorum profundus tendon
Proximal median neuropathy or pronator syndrome (which includes sensory symptoms)
Attritional tendon rupture in rheumatoid arthritis (Mannerfelt lesion)
Flexor tendon adhesion or Volkmann ischaemic contracture
additionalInvestigations: Needle electromyography of flexor pollicis longus, flexor digitorum profundus to the index and pronator quadratus with sparing of other median muscles
Nerve conduction studies to confirm normal median sensory responses and exclude a more proximal lesion
Tenodesis test and passive wrist movement to confirm tendon integrity
High-resolution ultrasound or MRI neurography seeking hourglass fascicular constrictions or a compressive lesion
MRI of the proximal forearm if a mass or anomalous muscle is suspected
Assessment for antecedent viral illness, immunisation or surgery supporting neuralgic amyotrophy
redFlags: Acute severe shoulder-girdle or forearm pain preceding weakness, indicating neuralgic amyotrophy
Inability to flex the distal joints of thumb and index with an intact tenodesis effect, distinguishing palsy from tendon rupture
A palpable or imaged mass in the proximal forearm
reference.prognosis: Cases due to neuralgic amyotrophy and to relieved compression frequently recover useful pinch function over several months to about a year, though recovery can be incomplete. Persistent deficits from unresolved fascicular constriction or structural compression may benefit from surgical exploration, nerve reconstruction or tendon transfer.
pitfalls: Mistaking the palsy for flexor tendon rupture by not checking the tenodesis effect
Overlooking neuralgic amyotrophy as the underlying mechanism in painful acute presentations
Rushing to surgical decompression before allowing time for spontaneous recovery in inflammatory cases
Confusing it with carpal tunnel or pronator syndrome despite the complete absence of sensory symptoms
Failing to isolate pronator quadratus by testing pronation with the elbow flexed
management: In neuralgic amyotrophy, control the acute severe pain with analgesia and consider early corticosteroids
Manage most cases conservatively with observation and physiotherapy, as spontaneous recovery over months is common
Provide hand therapy with splinting, range-of-motion exercises, and functional pinch retraining
Monitor recovery with serial clinical and electrophysiological assessment

Undertake surgical exploration with nerve decompression or interfascicular neurolysis when there is no recovery or a structural compressive cause such as a fibrous band, accessory flexor pollicis longus head, or mass
Consider tendon transfers for persistent disabling loss of pinch
